name: Saskatchewan
summary_text: Saskatchewan stands under the framework of Canada, where gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code as amended by Bill C-16, passed by the Senate 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, most provinces permit a change of the gender marker on official documents by declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction.  Provincial policy in Saskatchewan runs against that current. Saskatchewan and Alberta are the two provinces that have enacted rollbacks affecting trans people, and Saskatchewan's is anchored in schools. On 22 August 2023 the Government of Saskatchewan's education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring schools to obtain parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, to inform parents about the sexual-health curriculum, and pausing third-party school programs. The announcement prompted a court challenge that has now reached Canada's highest court, and no ruling on the merits has altered the policy: the parental-consent requirement has been in force since 2023.  The litigation has produced a split record. On 11 August 2025, in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74, the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan set aside the 2023 chambers decision, holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test sections 1 and 15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where section 33 was invoked, so the policy stands; in the same decision the court granted the province's appeal in part and held that a judge does have jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, allowing UR Pride's litigation to continue in the Court of King's Bench. Amnesty International Canada, an intervenor, called the ruling a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights, arguing that use of the override clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it would hear the appeals, with both the province and UR Pride seeking expedited hearings alongside a challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before the country's highest court.  Conditions in custody are the weakest point for a trans visitor who is detained. The Correctional Service of Canada has, since 2018, accommodated offenders on the basis of gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement in a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, refusing a request only where overriding health or safety concerns cannot be resolved. The reality lags the policy: as of 2025, of 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 were housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator's 2022-23 report welcomed the 2022 gender-diversity policy but flagged the unclear parameters of the override and the absence of any dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

name: Yukon
summary_text: Yukon stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.  Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Healthcare coverage is universal.  National crime data bear directly on what a trans visitor can expect. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (30 March 2026) recorded 4,882 police-reported hate crimes in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023 and 169% above 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and 184% above the 2020 figure. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113 incidents against a monthly average near 50. The same release shows police-reported hate-crime rates roughly 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), a gap that bears on a sparsely populated territory where reporting infrastructure is thinner.  The figures available for this territory are national rather than local. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines police-reported data with gender identity or expression and sexual-orientation motivations, but its numbers are national and do not report Yukon-level victimisation.  Official recognition in the territory itself is on the record. The Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2026, with MLAs rising to speak; Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Klune) praised the courage, resilience and contributions of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, acknowledged that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt.  Hostility at the local level has also surfaced. In June 2024 a Pride flag was allegedly vandalised and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend, and a replacement flag was promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June 2024, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy, SOGI 123, saying Pride month celebrates the diversity that makes the Yukon vibrant and strong.
